subject: cmimc_2025
sample_text:
Let
\[
S=\sum_{x=1}^{25}(f(f(x))-x)^2.
\]
For a uniformly random function, the values \(f(1),\ldots,f(25)\) are independent and uniform on \(\{1,\ldots,25\}\).

Fix \(x\) and condition on \(f(x)=y\):
- If \(y=x\), then \(f(f(x))=x\), so the contribution is \(0\).
- If \(y\ne x\), then \(f(y)\) is independent of \(f(x)\) and uniform. Thus the conditional expected contribution is
  \[
  \frac1{25}\sum_{z=1}^{25}(z-x)^2.
  \]

Since \(\Pr(f(x)\ne x)=24/25\), linearity of expectation gives
\[
\mathbb E[S]=\frac{24}{625}\sum_{x=1}^{25}\sum_{z=1}^{25}(z-x)^2.
\]
Expanding the square,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{x=1}^{25}\sum_{z=1}^{25}(z-x)^2
&=50\sum_{x=1}^{25}x^2-2\left(\sum_{x=1}^{25}x\right)^2\\
&=50\left(\frac{25\cdot26\cdot51}{6}\right)
-2\left(\frac{25\cdot26}{2}\right)^2\\
&=276250-211250\\
&=65000.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore the expected value is
\[
\frac{24}{625}\cdot65000=\boxed{2496}.
\]

subject: cmimc_2025
sample_text:
Write the four corners of the square as
\[
A=(0,0),\quad B=(10,0),\quad C=(10,10),\quad D=(0,10),
\]
and the interior points as \(P=(3,4)\) and \(Q=(6,2)\). These names are just for organizing the calculation; assigning the original labels allows any ordering of the six points.

In a simple polygon, the vertices on its convex hull occur in their cyclic hull order. Thus, after reversing the orientation if necessary, the corner order is \(A,B,C,D\). We only need to insert \(P\) and \(Q\) into the four gaps between successive corners.

### 1. Calculate the possible areas
The square has area \(100\). Inserting an interior point \(X\) between consecutive corners \(U,V\) reduces the area by \([UVX]\). These reductions are
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrr}
&AB&BC&CD&DA\\ \hline
P&20&35&30&15\\
Q&10&20&40&30
\end{array}
\]

If \(P\) and \(Q\) lie in different gaps, subtract their two reductions from \(100\).

If both lie in the same gap \(UV\), compute the areas for the two chains \(U,P,Q,V\) and \(U,Q,P,V\) using the shoelace formula. For example, the orders
\[
A,P,Q,B,C,D\quad\text{and}\quad A,Q,P,B,C,D
\]
give areas \(81\) and \(89\), respectively.

The complete table of candidate areas is therefore
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrr}
\text{gap containing }P\backslash\text{gap containing }Q
&AB&BC&CD&DA\\ \hline
AB&81,\ 89&60&40&50\\
BC&55&81,\ 64&25&35\\
CD&60&50&76,\ 54&40\\
DA&75&65&45&76,\ 79
\end{array}
\]
Some entries correspond to self-intersecting polygons, so they must be excluded.

### 2. Find the maximum
Every entry is at most \(89\), and
\[
A,Q,P,B,C,D
\]
is non-self-intersecting. Hence
\[
a_{\max}=89.
\]

### 3. Find the minimum
The only candidate areas below \(45\) are \(25,35\), and the two occurrences of \(40\). Each forces a crossing:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
P\text{ gap}&Q\text{ gap}&\text{crossing edges}\\ \hline
AB&CD&BP,\ QD\\
BC&CD&BP,\ CQ\\
BC&DA&PC,\ DQ\\
CD&DA&CP,\ DQ
\end{array}
\]
Indeed, the respective intersection points are
\[
\left(\frac{45}{8},\frac52\right),\qquad
\left(\frac{55}{9},\frac{20}{9}\right),\qquad
\left(\frac{90}{23},\frac{110}{23}\right),
\]
with the last point applying to both final rows. Each lies strictly inside both indicated segments.

Meanwhile, \(A,B,C,Q,D,P\) is non-self-intersecting and has area
\[
\frac12\left(100-40+60-30\right)=45.
\]
Thus \(a_{\min}=45\), and the requested difference is
\[
\boxed{44}.
\]

subject: smt_2025
sample_text:
Let \(\theta\in(0,\pi)\) be the common colatitude of \(B\) and \(C\), so their common \(z\)-coordinate is \(\cos\theta\). Let \(\phi\in(0,\pi]\) be their smaller longitude separation.

The arcs \(AB\) and \(AC\) are meridian arcs, each of length \(\theta\). The latitude circle through \(B\) and \(C\) has radius \(\sin\theta\), so the minor arc \(BC\) has length \(\phi\sin\theta\). Thus the total length is
\[
L=2\theta+\phi\sin\theta.
\]

The region between these two meridians, from the north pole down to colatitude \(\theta\), has area
\[
\int_0^\phi\int_0^\theta \sin t\,dt\,d\lambda
=\phi(1-\cos\theta).
\]
Since \(\phi\le\pi\) and \(\theta<\pi\), this area is less than \(2\pi\), half the sphere’s area. Therefore it is indeed the smaller enclosed region, and
\[
\phi(1-\cos\theta)=3.
\]
Substituting into the length formula gives
\[
L=2\theta+\frac{3\sin\theta}{1-\cos\theta}
=2\theta+3\cot\frac{\theta}{2}.
\]

Differentiate:
\[
L'(\theta)=2-\frac32\csc^2\frac{\theta}{2}.
\]
Because \(\sin(\theta/2)\) increases on \((0,\pi)\), this derivative changes from negative to positive when
\[
\sin^2\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac34,
\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad
\theta=\frac{2\pi}{3}.
\]
This is the global minimum on \((0,\pi)\). It is feasible: at this colatitude,
\[
\phi=\frac{3}{1-\cos(2\pi/3)}=2<\pi.
\]

Hence the minimum total arc length is
\[
2\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)+3\cot\frac{\pi}{3}
=\boxed{\frac{4\pi}{3}+\sqrt3}.
\]

subject: smt_2025
sample_text:
Put \(D=(0,0)\), with \(BC\) on the \(x\)-axis and \(A\) above it. Write
\[
\theta=\angle ADC,\qquad t=\cot\frac{\theta}{2}>0.
\]
The centers of the circles of radii \(5\) and \(7\) are then
\[
O_2=\left(-\frac5t,5\right),\qquad O_3=(7t,7).
\]
Thus their distance gives
\[
\left(7t+\frac5t\right)^2+(7-5)^2=13^2,
\]
so
\[
7t+\frac5t=\sqrt{165}.
\]
Consequently, the two possible values of \(t\) satisfy
\[
7t^2-\sqrt{165}\,t+5=0,
\qquad
t=\frac{\sqrt{165}\pm5}{14}. \tag{1}
\]

We next establish the inradius corresponding to each value of \(t\).

### A radius identity
More generally, suppose the two small circles have radii \(u,v\). We will show that the triangle’s inradius is
\[
r=\frac{u+vt^2}{1+t^2}. \tag{2}
\]

Let the circumcenter be \((h,k)\), its radius be \(R\), and put
\[
q=R-k,\qquad p=R^2-h^2-k^2.
\]
Since \(D\) lies inside the circumcircle, \(p>0\). Internal tangency of the two small circles to the circumcircle yields
\[
p=2u\left(q+\frac ht\right)+\frac{u^2}{t^2},
\qquad
p=2v(q-ht)+v^2t^2.
\]
Define
\[
s=\frac ut+vt,\qquad \rho=\frac{u+vt^2}{1+t^2}.
\]
Solving the preceding equations gives
\[
h=\frac{(v-u)q}{s}+\frac{vt-u/t}{2},
\qquad
p=uv+\frac{2uvq}{\rho}. \tag{3}
\]

Write \(A=(wy,y)\), where
\[
w=\cot\theta=\frac{t^2-1}{2t}.
\]
The circumcircle equation at \(A\) is
\[
(1+w^2)y^2-2(hw+k)y-p=0.
\]
Using (3) and
\[
k=\frac{h^2+p-q^2}{2q},
\]
this factors as
\[
(1+w^2)
\left(y-2\rho-\frac{\rho^2}{q}\right)
\left(y+\frac{4uvq}{s^2}\right)=0.
\]
Because \(y>0\), we obtain
\[
y=2\rho+\frac{\rho^2}{q}. \tag{4}
\]

To relate this height to the inradius, let \(a=BC\) and let \(r\) be the inradius. The standard chord and area identities give
\[
a^2=4(R^2-k^2)=4q(R+k),
\qquad AB\cdot AC=2Ry.
\]
Since \(\cos A=k/R\),
\[
(AB+AC)^2=a^2+4(R+k)y.
\]
Also, the area formula gives
\[
r=\frac{ay}{a+AB+AC}.
\]
Combining these equations simplifies to
\[
y=2r+\frac{r^2}{q}.
\]
The expression on the right is strictly increasing for \(r>0\). Comparing with (4) proves (2).

### Summing the two possibilities
Here \(u=5\) and \(v=7\), so
\[
r=\frac{5+7t^2}{1+t^2}
=7-\frac{2}{1+t^2}.
\]
Let the roots of (1) be \(t_1,t_2\). By Vieta’s formulas,
\[
t_1+t_2=\frac{\sqrt{165}}7,\qquad t_1t_2=\frac57,
\]
and hence
\[
t_1^2+t_2^2=\frac{95}{49}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac1{1+t_1^2}+\frac1{1+t_2^2}
=
\frac{2+t_1^2+t_2^2}
{1+t_1^2+t_2^2+t_1^2t_2^2}
=\frac{193}{169}.
\]
Both roots are attainable: for example, choosing \(q=10\) in the construction above gives, for either root, an acute triangle with all four line-tangency points on the required segments.

Thus the sum of all possible inradii is
\[
14-2\cdot\frac{193}{169}
=\boxed{\frac{1980}{169}}.
\]

subject: hmmt_nov_2025
sample_text:
First, \(c\ge 0\). If \(c=0\), the equation is quadratic and has at most two distinct solutions, so \(c>0\).

Split the equation into
\[
x^2+ax+b-c=0
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
x^2+ax+b+c=0.
\]
Their solution sets are disjoint. Moreover, if a monic quadratic with integer coefficients has one integer root \(r\), its other root is \(-a-r\), also an integer. Thus, to obtain exactly three distinct integer solutions, one quadratic must have a double integer root and the other must have two distinct integer roots.

The discriminants are
\[
D_1=a^2-4b+4c,\qquad D_2=a^2-4b-4c,
\]
with \(D_1>D_2\). The double root must therefore come from \(D_2=0\); otherwise \(D_1=0\) would give \(D_2<0\).

Since the double root is \(-a/2\), write \(a=2m\). Then \(D_2=0\) gives \(b=m^2-c\), so the original equation becomes
\[
\left|(x+m)^2-c\right|=c.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
(x+m)^2=0\qquad\text{or}\qquad (x+m)^2=2c.
\]
There are exactly three distinct integer solutions precisely when \(2c\) is a positive perfect square. Its square root must be even, so
\[
c=2n^2,\qquad n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}.
\]

Every such value works, for example by choosing \(a=0\) and \(b=-2n^2\), yielding the solutions \(0,\pm2n\).

Finally,
\[
2(31)^2=1922\le2025,\qquad 2(32)^2=2048>2025.
\]
Hence \(n=1,2,\ldots,31\), giving
\[
\boxed{31}.
\]

subject: hmmt_feb_2026
sample_text:
Any qualifying integer has at least four digits. We first rule out four- and five-digit possibilities.

Since
\[
2026\equiv 6\pmod{101},
\]
the four-digit number \(2026\) does not qualify. A five-digit number containing \(2026\) has one of two forms:
- \(2026d=20260+d\), whose remainder modulo \(101\) is \(60+d\), between \(60\) and \(69\);
- \(d2026=10000d+2026\), whose remainder is \(d+6\), between \(7\) and \(15\), because \(10000\equiv1\pmod{101}\).

Thus no qualifying number has fewer than six digits.

For six digits, the block \(2026\) can occupy exactly three positions:

1. **\(2026ab\):** Write the number as \(202600+t\), where \(0\le t\le99\). Since
   \[
   202600+t\equiv95+t\pmod{101},
   \]
   divisibility requires \(t=6\), giving \(202606\).

2. **\(a2026b\):** Here \(1\le a\le9\) and \(0\le b\le9\). Since \(100000\equiv10\pmod{101}\),
   \[
   100000a+20260+b\equiv10a+60+b\pmod{101}.
   \]
   This expression lies between \(70\) and \(159\), so it must equal \(101\). Hence \(10a+b=41\), giving \(420261\).

3. **\(ab2026\):** Write the two-digit prefix as \(k\), where \(10\le k\le99\). Then
   \[
   10000k+2026\equiv k+6\pmod{101},
   \]
   so \(k=95\), giving \(952026\).

The qualifying six-digit numbers, in increasing order, are
\[
202606<420261<952026.
\]
As a check, \(420261=101\cdot4161\). Therefore the second smallest is
\[
\boxed{420261}.
\]

sample_text:
Let the circumradius of the original regular \(24\)-gon be \(R\).

A chord \(\overline{A_iA_{i+k}}\) subtends a central angle of
\[
\frac{360^\circ k}{24}=15^\circ k.
\]
The perpendicular from the center bisects the chord, so its distance from the center is
\[
R\cos\left(\frac{15^\circ k}{2}\right).
\]
The \(24\) chords are rotations of one another by \(15^\circ\), and their lines bound the central regular \(24\)-gon. Thus this distance is its apothem.

For the two configurations, the apothems are therefore
\[
r_1=R\cos67.5^\circ=R\sin22.5^\circ,
\qquad
r_2=R\cos82.5^\circ=R\sin7.5^\circ.
\]

Since the two central polygons are similar, their area ratio is
\[
\frac{K_1}{K_2}
=\left(\frac{\sin22.5^\circ}{\sin7.5^\circ}\right)^2.
\]
Using \(\sin3x=3\sin x-4\sin^3x\) with \(x=7.5^\circ\),
\[
\frac{\sin22.5^\circ}{\sin7.5^\circ}
=3-4\sin^27.5^\circ
=1+2\cos15^\circ
=1+\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{2}.
\]
Hence
\[
\frac{K_1}{K_2}
=\left(1+\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{2}\right)^2
=\boxed{3+\sqrt2+\sqrt3+\sqrt6}.
\]

subject: hmmt_nov_2025
sample_text:
Let \(AB=x\) and \(CD=y\). Since \(AD=39\) and \(BC=10\),
\[
x+y=29.
\]

Place the points at
\[
A=(-x,0),\quad B=(0,0),\quad C=(10,0),\quad D=(10+y,0).
\]
Because \(BEC\) is equilateral, we may take \(E=(5,5\sqrt3)\).

Set \(p=x+5\) and \(q=y+5\), so \(p+q=39\). The vectors from \(E\) to \(A\) and \(D\) are
\[
\overrightarrow{EA}=(-p,-5\sqrt3),\qquad
\overrightarrow{ED}=(q,-5\sqrt3).
\]
Using \(\angle AED=120^\circ\),
\[
\frac{75-pq}{\sqrt{(p^2+75)(q^2+75)}}=-\frac12.
\]
Write \(P=pq\). Squaring and using \(p^2+q^2=39^2-2P\) gives
\[
4(P-75)^2=P^2+75(39^2-2P)+75^2.
\]
Simplifying,
\[
P^2-150P-32400=0,
\qquad
(P-270)(P+120)=0.
\]

subject: smt_2025
sample_text:
Let the roots be \(a,b,d\). By Vieta’s formulas,
\[
a+b+d=0,\qquad ab+ad+bd=-147,\qquad abd=-c.
\]

First, the roots must be real. Otherwise, there is one real root of absolute value \(p\) and a conjugate pair of absolute value \(q\), where \(p,q\) are primes. The conjugate pair has sum equal to the negative of the real root and product \(q^2\), so
\[
q^2-p^2=-147.
\]
Thus \(p^2-q^2=147\). Since this is odd, \(p,q\) have opposite parity. As \(p>q\), we must have \(q=2\), giving \(p^2=151\), which is impossible.

Now all three roots are signed primes. Their sum is zero, so the absolute value of the root with the lone sign equals the sum of the other two absolute values. Write these primes as
\[
r=p+q.
\]
If both \(p,q\) were odd, \(r\) would be even and greater than \(2\), hence not prime. Therefore one is \(2\); take \(p=2\), so \(r=q+2\).

Up to reversing all signs, the roots are \(2,q,-(q+2)\). Consequently,
\[
-147=2q-2(q+2)-q(q+2)
=-q^2-2q-4.
\]
Hence
\[
q^2+2q-143=(q-11)(q+13)=0,
\]
so \(q=11\) and \(r=13\). These are indeed primes, and
\[
|c|=|abd|=2\cdot11\cdot13=\boxed{286}.
\]

subject: brumo_2025
sample_text:
Let \(AB=AC=s\). Take \(A\) as the origin, and write
\[
B=\mathbf u,\qquad C=\mathbf v,\qquad
G=x\mathbf u,\qquad H=y\mathbf v,
\]
where \(|\mathbf u|=|\mathbf v|=s\).

Since \(D\) lies on minor arc \(AB\), it is on the opposite side of \(AB\) from \(C\). Thus the points on the chord \(DI\) occur in the order
\[
D,\ G,\ H,\ I.
\]
Consequently, \(GI=6\), \(HD=8\), and \(DI=9\).

### 1. Use power of a point
At \(G\) and \(H\), respectively,
\[
GA\cdot GB=GD\cdot GI=18,
\qquad
HA\cdot HC=HD\cdot HI=8.
\]
Therefore
\[
s^2x(1-x)=18,\qquad s^2y(1-y)=8. \tag{1}
\]

Because \(DG=3\) and \(GH=5\),
\[
D=G-\frac35(H-G)
=\frac{8x}{5}\mathbf u-\frac{3y}{5}\mathbf v. \tag{2}
\]

### 2. Use the midpoint condition
Write \(E=p\mathbf u+q\mathbf v\). Since \(E\) lies on line \(BC\),
\[
p+q=1.
\]
Also, \(E,G,F\) are collinear and \(F=\frac12\mathbf v\). Comparing coefficients in
\[
G=F+t(E-F)
\]
gives
\[
x=tp,\qquad 0=\frac12+t\left(q-\frac12\right).
\]
Eliminating \(t\), using \(p+q=1\), yields
\[
\frac qp=\frac{x-1}{x}.
\]

Since \(A,D,E\) are collinear, equation (2) now gives
\[
-\frac{3y}{8x}=\frac{x-1}{x},
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
y=\frac83(1-x). \tag{3}
\]

Divide the two equations in (1) and substitute (3):
\[
\frac{y(1-y)}{x(1-x)}=\frac49
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{8(8x-5)}{9x}=\frac49.
\]
Hence
\[
x=\frac23,\qquad y=\frac89.
\]
Equation (1) then gives
\[
s^2\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac13=18,
\qquad s=9.
\]

### 3. Compute \(AE\)
Let \(c=\cos\angle BAC\), so \(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=81c\). From \(GH=5\),
\[
25=\left|\frac89\mathbf v-\frac23\mathbf u\right|^2
=100-96c,
\]
which gives
\[
c=\frac{25}{32}.
\]

The equations for \(p,q\), with \(x=\frac23\), give \(p=2\), \(q=-1\). Thus
\[
E=2\mathbf u-\mathbf v,
\]
and
\[
AE^2=|2\mathbf u-\mathbf v|^2
=81(5-4c)
=81\left(5-\frac{25}{8}\right)
=\frac{1215}{8}.
\]

Therefore the requested length is
\[
\boxed{\frac{9\sqrt{30}}{4}}.
\]

x^2+16x+48=(x+4)(x+12),\qquad
x^2+24x+128=(x+8)(x+16).

(y+6)(y-2)(y+2)(y-6)=44^{2^{2025}},

subject: hmmt_feb_2026
sample_text:
Since the sixth largest divisor is \(6\), exactly five divisors of \(n\) are greater than \(6\), and \(6\mid n\).

The divisors of \(n\) that are at most \(6\) always include \(1,2,3,6\). The only other possibilities are \(4\) and \(5\). Thus, writing \(\tau(n)\) for the number of positive divisors,
\[
\tau(n)=9+\mathbf 1_{4\mid n}+\mathbf 1_{5\mid n},
\]
so \(\tau(n)\in\{9,10,11\}\).

If \(n=\prod p_i^{a_i}\), then \(\tau(n)=\prod(a_i+1)\). We consider each possibility:

- **\(\tau(n)=9\):** The prime factorization has the form \(p^8\) or \(p^2q^2\). Since \(6\mid n\), only \(n=2^2 3^2=36\) is possible. But \(4\mid36\), so the displayed formula would require \(\tau(36)=10\), a contradiction.

- **\(\tau(n)=10\):** The form is \(p^9\) or \(p^4q\). Since \(6\mid n\), the candidates are
  \[
  n=2^4\cdot3=48,\qquad n=2\cdot3^4=162.
  \]
  Exactly one of \(4,5\) must divide \(n\). This holds for \(48\), but not for \(162\).

- **\(\tau(n)=11\):** Since \(11\) is prime, \(n=p^{10}\), which cannot be divisible by \(6\).

Finally, the divisors of \(48\) in decreasing order are
\[
48,24,16,12,8,6,4,3,2,1,
\]
so its sixth largest divisor is indeed \(6\). Therefore the requested sum is
\[
\boxed{48}.
\]

subject: hmmt_nov_2025
sample_text:
Kelvin must make exactly three moves increasing \(x\) and three moves increasing \(y\). Their order can be chosen in
\[
\binom{6}{3}=20
\]
ways.

Fix one such order. These six horizontal moves take Kelvin through seven distinct \((x,y)\)-positions. At each fixed \((x,y)\), his vertical moves must all go in the same direction: reversing direction would immediately revisit a point. Thus, between any two specified heights, there is exactly one permitted vertical segment.

Now choose the height at which each of the six horizontal moves occurs. Each height can independently be any of
\[
0,1,2,3,
\]
giving \(4^6\) choices. Every choice produces a valid path: move vertically from height \(0\) to the first chosen height, follow the prescribed horizontal moves with vertical segments between them, and finally move vertically to height \(3\).

No point is repeated within a vertical segment, and different segments have different \((x,y)\)-positions. Conversely, every valid path determines exactly one horizontal order and one sequence of six heights.

Therefore, the number of paths is
\[
\binom{6}{3}4^6=20\cdot4096=\boxed{81920}.
\]

subject: cmimc_2025
sample_text:
Work modulo \(3\). Since
\[
1+x+x^2\equiv(1-x)^2\pmod3,
\]
we have
\[
(1+x+x^2)^{2024}\equiv(1-x)^{4048}\pmod3.
\]

The base-\(3\) expansion of \(4048\) is
\[
4048=(12112221)_3.
\]
Using \((1-x)^{3^j}\equiv1-x^{3^j}\pmod3\), we obtain
\[
(1-x)^{4048}\equiv
\prod_{j=0}^{7}(1-x^{3^j})^{d_j}\pmod3,
\]
where the \(d_j\) are the ternary digits of \(4048\): four are \(1\), and four are \(2\).

For each digit:
- If \(d_j=1\), the factor is \(1-x^{3^j}\), so the exponent digit can be \(0\) or \(1\), with coefficient \(1\) or \(-1\), respectively.
- If \(d_j=2\), the factor is
  \[
  (1-x^{3^j})^2\equiv1+x^{3^j}+x^{2\cdot3^j}\pmod3,
  \]
  so the exponent digit can be \(0,1,\) or \(2\), each with coefficient \(1\).

These choices give distinct exponents by uniqueness of ternary representation, and all lie between \(0\) and \(4048\). Thus a coefficient equals \(1\) modulo \(3\) precisely when an even number of the four digit-\(1\) factors contribute their negative term.

There are
\[
\binom40+\binom42+\binom44=8
\]
such choices, and the four digit-\(2\) factors independently give \(3^4\) choices. Therefore the required number is
\[
8\cdot3^4=\boxed{648}.
\]

subject: smt_2025
sample_text:
Assign coordinates to the grid vertices, with bottom-left \((0,0)\) and top-right \((3,3)\).

A diagonal preserves the parity of \(x+y\), so a path starting at \((0,0)\) can visit only vertices where \(x+y\) is even. In each cell, exactly one diagonal connects such vertices; call it the **usable diagonal**.

The bottom-left and top-right cells must have their usable diagonals drawn, since these are the only ways to leave \((0,0)\) and reach \((3,3)\). Thus, we need a connection from \((1,1)\) to \((2,2)\) using the seven remaining cells.

There are exactly three possible routes between these vertices:
- The central diagonal, directly from \((1,1)\) to \((2,2)\).
- The three-diagonal route
  \[
  (1,1)\to(0,2)\to(1,3)\to(2,2).
  \]
- The three-diagonal route
  \[
  (1,1)\to(2,0)\to(3,1)\to(2,2).
  \]

These routes use disjoint sets of cells.

If the central diagonal is usable, all six other cells are arbitrary, giving \(2^6=64\) choices.

If the central diagonal is not usable, at least one of the two three-diagonal routes must be complete. Each complete route leaves the other three cells arbitrary, so inclusion–exclusion gives
\[
2^3+2^3-1=15
\]
choices.

Therefore, the required number is
\[
\boxed{79}.
\]

subject: hmmt_nov_2025
sample_text:
Let \(\tau(M)\) be the number of positive divisors of \(M\). The pairing
\[
d\longleftrightarrow \frac{M}{d}
\]
shows that the number of divisors satisfying \(d\ge M/100\) equals the number of divisors of \(M\) that are at most \(100\). Denote this number by \(B(M)\).

Thus \(M\) is imbalanced precisely when
\[
\tau(M)-B(M)>\frac{99}{100}\tau(M),
\qquad\text{or equivalently}\qquad
\tau(M)>100B(M).
\]

Since \(2000=2^4\cdot5^3\) divides \(M\), the following thirteen numbers all divide \(M\):
\[
1,2,4,8,16;\qquad 5,10,20,40,80;\qquad 25,50,100.
\]
Therefore \(B(M)\ge13\), so \(\tau(M)>1300\).

Now let \(a\ge4\) be the exponent of \(2\) in \(M\).
- If \(a=4\), then \(5\mid\tau(M)\). The smallest multiple of \(5\) strictly greater than \(1300\) is \(1305\).
- If \(a\ge5\), then \(32\) is an additional divisor at most \(100\). Hence \(B(M)\ge14\), giving \(\tau(M)>1400\).

Consequently, every imbalanced multiple of \(2000\) has at least \(1305\) divisors.

To attain this bound, take
\[
M=2^4\cdot5^{260}.
\]
It has
\[
\tau(M)=(4+1)(260+1)=1305.
\]
Its divisors at most \(100\) are exactly the thirteen listed above, because \(5^3>100\). Since \(1305>100\cdot13\), this \(M\) is imbalanced.

The minimum possible number of positive divisors is
\[
\boxed{1305}.
\]

If \(x\) is a positive integer \(k\), then
\[
x(\lceil x\rceil+\lfloor x\rfloor)=2k^2.

Since \(2\cdot31^2=1922\le2025<2048=2\cdot32^2\), this gives \(31\) representable integers.

If \(x\) is not an integer, write \(k=\lfloor x\rfloor\), so \(k<x<k+1\). Then
\[
x(\lceil x\rceil+\lfloor x\rfloor)=(2k+1)x,
\]
which takes every value in the open interval
\[
\bigl(k(2k+1),(k+1)(2k+1)\bigr).
\]
Both endpoints are integers, so this interval contains exactly
\[
(k+1)(2k+1)-k(2k+1)-1=2k

integers.

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{31}2k=31\cdot32=992

integers.

subject: hmmt_feb_2026
sample_text:
Let \(k=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\) and \(A=(k!)^{n!}\). We seek the largest \(n\) such that \(n\mid A+450\).

### 1. Restrict the prime factors of \(n\)

Suppose \(p^e\mid n\), where \(p\le k\). Since \(p\mid k!\),
\[
v_p(A)=n!\,v_p(k!)\ge n!\ge e,
\]
so \(p^e\mid A\). Hence the required divisibility implies
\[
p^e\mid450.
\]

Any prime factor \(p>k\) satisfies \(p>\sqrt n\). There can be at most one such prime factor, and its exponent must be \(1\).

Thus either \(n\mid450\), giving \(n\le450\), or
\[
n=mp,\qquad m\mid450,\qquad p>\sqrt n.
\]
In the latter case, \(p^2>mp\), so \(m<p\).

### 2. Determine the possible large prime

Because \(p>k\), we have \(p\nmid k!\). Also, \(p-1\le n\), so \(p-1\mid n!\). Fermat’s little theorem therefore gives
\[
A=(k!)^{n!}\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
Consequently,
\[
p\mid A+450\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p\mid451=11\cdot41.
\]
Thus \(p\in\{11,41\}\).

- If \(p=11\), then \(m<11\), so \(n=11m\le110\).
- If \(p=41\), then \(m<41\) and \(m\mid450\). The divisors of \(450\) below \(41\) are
  \[
  1,2,3,5,6,9,10,15,18,25,30.
  \]
  Therefore \(n\le41\cdot30=1230\).

### 3. Verify the upper bound

For \(n=1230=30\cdot41\),
\[
35^2<1230<36^2,
\]
so \(k=35\). Since \(30\mid35!\) and \(30\mid450\),
\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv0\pmod{30}.
\]
Also, \(41\nmid35!\) and \(40\mid1230!\), so
\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv1+450=451\equiv0\pmod{41}.
\]
Since \(\gcd(30,41)=1\), the expression is divisible by \(1230\).

Hence the largest possible integer is
\[
\boxed{1230}.
\]

sample_text:

\[

\]
Using the standard trigonometric identities, this becomes
\[
2i\bigl(\sin4\theta+\cos2\theta-\sin\theta-\cos\theta\bigr)=0.
\]
Thus we need to solve
\[
\sin4\theta+\cos2\theta-\sin\theta-\cos\theta=0.
\]

\[
t=\sin\theta+\cos\theta,\qquad d=\cos\theta-\sin\theta.
\]
Then
\[
\sin2\theta=t^2-1,\qquad \cos2\theta=td,\qquad t^2+d^2=2.
\]
Consequently, the equation factors as
\[
\begin{aligned}
0
&=\cos2\theta(2\sin2\theta+1)-t\\
&=t\bigl(d(2t^2-1)-1\bigr)\\
&=t\bigl(d(3-2d^2)-1\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore either \(t=0\), or
\[
2d^3-3d+1=(d-1)(2d^2+2d-1)=0.
\]

- If \(t=0\), then \(\sin\theta+\cos\theta=0\), giving
  \[
  \theta=\frac{3\pi}{4}.

- If \(d=1\), then \(\cos\theta-\sin\theta=1\), giving

  \theta=0.

- If \(d=\dfrac{\sqrt3-1}{2}\), then

- If \(d=-\dfrac{\sqrt3+1}{2}\), then

  \]

These lists are exhaustive because
\[
d=\sqrt2\cos\left(\theta+\frac{\pi}{4}\right),
\qquad
\theta+\frac{\pi}{4}\in\left[\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{5\pi}{4}\right).
\]

All five angles are distinct, so their sum is
\[

=\boxed{\frac{29\pi}{12}}.

subject: cmimc_2025
sample_text:
Let \(n=2024\). Associate to the coloring a bipartite graph with vertices
\[
R_1,\ldots,R_n,\qquad C_1,\ldots,C_n,
\]
representing the rows and columns. Include the edge \(R_iC_j\) exactly when square \((i,j)\) is black.

### 1. Simple colorings correspond to forests

Suppose the graph contains a cycle. Its edges correspond to black squares that lie alternately in a common row and a common column. The ant can travel between these squares, turning at each one, and return to its starting square. Thus the coloring is not simple.

Conversely, suppose the ant makes a closed walk. Record only the squares where it turns. Consecutive turning squares share alternately a row and a column, so their corresponding edges form a closed walk in the bipartite graph. This graph walk never immediately retraces an edge: such a retracing would mean that two consecutive turns occurred at the same square.

But every nonempty closed walk in a forest must immediately retrace an edge somewhere. Therefore the graph contains a cycle.

Hence a coloring is simple precisely when its graph is a forest.

### 2. Maximal simple colorings correspond to spanning trees

Adding a black square means adding an edge of \(K_{n,n}\). A spanning tree is a maximal forest, since every additional edge creates a cycle.

Conversely, if a forest is disconnected, some edge of the connected graph \(K_{n,n}\) joins two of its components. Adding this edge does not create a cycle, so the coloring is not maximal.

Thus we must count the spanning trees of \(K_{n,n}\).

### 3. Count the spanning trees

By the Matrix–Tree Theorem, this number is the determinant of a reduced Laplacian. Deleting one column-vertex gives
\[
M=
\begin{pmatrix}
nI_n & -J_{n,n-1}\\
-J_{n-1,n} & nI_{n-1}
\end{pmatrix},
\]
where \(J\) denotes an all-ones matrix.

Taking the Schur complement,
\[
\det M
=n^{n-1}\det\left(nI_n-\frac{n-1}{n}J_{n,n}\right).
\]
The matrix \(J_{n,n}\) has eigenvalue \(n\) once and eigenvalue \(0\) with multiplicity \(n-1\). Therefore the matrix inside the determinant has eigenvalues \(1\) once and \(n\) with multiplicity \(n-1\). Consequently,
\[
\det M=n^{n-1}n^{n-1}=n^{2n-2}.
\]

Substituting \(n=2024\), the required number is
\[
\boxed{2024^{4046}}.
\]

subject: hmmt_nov_2025
sample_text:
Rotate Bojac’s position \(90^\circ\) clockwise about the center of the grid, and call the resulting position \(B'\). This rotation preserves the grid and turns Bojac’s movement into the same direction as Jacob’s. Thus we may instead study **two people receiving identical movement instructions**, each staying still when blocked. Rotation is a bijection, so the number of distinct ordered pairs is unchanged.

### 1. Coordinate separations never increase

Label the coordinates \(0,1,\ldots,7\). Suppose the two horizontal coordinates are \(x_1\le x_2\). Under an East or West instruction:

- if both move, their separation stays unchanged;
- if one is blocked, their separation decreases by \(1\);
- once they coincide, they remain equal.

Their order therefore never reverses, and the same holds vertically.

Let the horizontal and vertical separations be \(a,b\), and define
\[
i=8-a,\qquad j=8-b.
\]
Both \(i\) and \(j\) are nondecreasing. Any instruction that changes them increases exactly one of them by \(1\).

For fixed separations \(a,b\) and fixed coordinate orders, there are
\[
(8-a)(8-b)=ij
\]
possible ordered position pairs: the smaller horizontal coordinate has \(8-a\) choices, and the smaller vertical coordinate has \(8-b\) choices.

### 2. An upper bound

Once the separations change, the previous separation pair cannot recur. Moreover, for each value \(s=i+j\), at most one separation pair can occur along a sequence.

For such a pair,
\[
ij\le \left\lfloor\frac{s^2}{4}\right\rfloor.
\]
Since \(2\le i+j\le16\), the total number of distinct ordered position pairs is at most
\[
\sum_{s=2}^{16}\left\lfloor\frac{s^2}{4}\right\rfloor
=\sum_{k=1}^{8}k^2+\sum_{k=1}^{7}k(k+1).
\]
These sums are
\[
204+168=372.
\]

### 3. Achieving the bound

Start Jacob and \(B'\) at opposite corners, so \(a=b=7\) and hence \((i,j)=(1,1)\). Decrease the separations alternately so that the successive layers are
\[
(1,1),(2,1),(2,2),(3,2),(3,3),\ldots,(8,7),(8,8).
\]

Within a fixed layer \((i,j)\), the possible ordered position pairs form an \(i\times j\) rectangular grid. Moving both people together, without pushing either against a blocking boundary, allows movement between neighboring states in this rectangle. Thus we can visit every state in the layer and then finish at any desired state.

To advance to the next layer, finish at a boundary in the appropriate coordinate and give one further instruction toward that boundary. One person stays still while the other moves, decreasing the desired separation by \(1\). We can therefore visit all \(ij\) states in every listed layer.

The resulting total meets the upper bound, so the maximum is
\[
\boxed{372}
\]

sample_text:
Let \(m=\underline{bcd}\). Then \(\underline{abcd}=1000a+m\), so the given equality is
\[
\sqrt{1000a+m}=a\sqrt m.
\]
Squaring and rearranging gives
\[
1000a=(a^2-1)m.
\]
If \(a=1\), this is impossible. Thus \(a\in\{2,3,\ldots,9\}\).

Because \(\gcd(a,a^2-1)=1\), we must have
\[
a^2-1\mid 1000.
\]
For \(a=2,3,\ldots,9\), the possible values of \(a^2-1\) are
\[
3,\ 8,\ 15,\ 24,\ 35,\ 48,\ 63,\ 80.
\]
Only \(8\) divides \(1000\), so \(a=3\). Hence
\[
m=\frac{1000\cdot3}{8}=375.
\]
Checking, \(\sqrt{3375}=\sqrt{9\cdot375}=3\sqrt{375}\), as required.

Therefore the only possible four-digit number is \(\boxed{3375}\).

sample_text:
Let the initial volume of gallium in flask B be \(g\) liters.

To fill flask B, Mark pours \(1-g\) liters of mercury from A into B, leaving \(g\) liters of pure mercury in A. Since B now contains exactly one liter, its mercury fraction is \(1-g\).

Mixing B and pouring some of it out does not change its composition. Thus,
\[
1-g=0.30 \quad\Rightarrow\quad g=0.70.
\]

Flask A therefore contains \(0.70\) liters of pure mercury before the second pour. To fill it, Mark adds \(0.30\) liters of the mixture, which contains
\[
0.30(0.30)=0.09
\]
liters of mercury.

Hence the full one-liter flask A contains \(0.70+0.09=0.79\) liters of mercury, so
\[
\boxed{x=79}.
\]

sample_text:
For two integers \(a,b\) with \(d,e\) digits respectively, placing \(a\) before \(b\) is better precisely when
\[
a10^e+b>b10^d+a,
\]
or equivalently,
\[
\frac{a}{10^d-1}>\frac{b}{10^e-1}.
\]
Thus, sorting by decreasing value of \(\frac{a}{10^d-1}\) maximizes the concatenation: any adjacent pair out of this order can be swapped to increase the number.

The key for \(2025\) is \(\frac{2025}{9999}\). Hence a \(d\)-digit integer \(n\) appears before \(2025\) exactly when
\[
n>\frac{2025(10^d-1)}{9999}.
\]
We count these integers for each possible digit length:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|r}
d & \text{Integers appearing before }2025 & \text{Count}\\ \hline
1 & 2,\ldots,9 & 8\\
2 & 21,\ldots,99 & 79\\
3 & 203,\ldots,999 & 797\\
4 & 2026,\ldots,9999 & 7974\\
5 & 20252,\ldots,99999 & 79748
\end{array}
\]
The threshold is an integer only for \(d=4\), where it equals \(2025\), so no other integer ties with \(2025\).

There are therefore
\[
8+79+797+7974+79748=88606
\]
integers before \(2025\). Its index is one greater:
\[
\boxed{88607}
\]

sample_text:
Let
\[
a=\log_2 x,\qquad b=\log_2 y,\qquad c=\log_2 z,\qquad t=\log_2 3.
\]
Taking base-\(2\) logarithms of the three given equations yields
\[
ab+ac=8+4t,\qquad ab+bc=9+6t,\qquad ac+bc=5+10t.
\]
Adding the first two equations and subtracting the third gives
\[
2ab=12,
\]
so \(ab=6\). Similarly,
\[
ac=2+4t,\qquad bc=3+6t.
\]
Since these three products are positive, \(a,b,c\) all have the same sign. Also,
\[
\frac ab=\frac{ac}{bc}=\frac{2+4t}{3+6t}=\frac23.
\]
Together with \(ab=6\), this gives
\[
(a,b)=(2,3)\quad\text{or}\quad(-2,-3).
\]
Using \(ac=2+4t\), the corresponding values of \(c\) are \(1+2t\) and \(-(1+2t)\). Therefore
\[
xyz=2^{a+b+c}=2^{\pm(6+2t)}.
\]
As \(2^t=3\), these two possible values are
\[
2^6\cdot 3^2=576
\quad\text{and}\quad
\frac1{576}.
\]
Both arise from the derived solutions and satisfy the original equations. Thus the smallest possible value is
\[
\boxed{\frac1{576}}.
\]

       \equiv a_n+2+b_n.

Thus we can compute \(b_{n+1}\) by addition, then find \(a_{n+1}=b_{n+1}^{-1}\). The values computed below are all nonzero and different from \(396\), so these operations are valid.

Starting with \(a_0=b_0=1\), we obtain:
\[

n&a_n&b_n\\ \hline
0&1&1\\
1&298&4\\
2&286&304\\
3&340&195\\

For example, \(b_{14}\equiv353+9+2=364\), and \(364\cdot12\equiv1\), confirming \(a_{14}=12\).

Since \(a_{17}=a_6\) and each next term is uniquely determined, the block from \(a_6\) through \(a_{16}\) repeats with period \(11\). Also,

\]
so \(a_{2026}=a_{13}=9\), consistent with the given information.

subject: smt_2025
sample_text:
Let
\[
F(x)=\frac{x-a}{4},\qquad G(x)=\frac{x-b}{6},\qquad H(x)=\frac{x-c}{9}
\]
be the inverses of \(f,g,h\). The root of a composition of \(f,g,h\) is obtained by applying the corresponding inverse composition to \(0\).

Thus, if
\[
A_0=\{0\},\qquad A_{n+1}=F(A_n)\cup G(A_n)\cup H(A_n),
\]
then \(R(a,b,c)=|A_{20}|\).

We first establish a growth bound.

### 1. A cardinality lemma

**Claim.** If \(A\subset\mathbb R\) is finite with \(|A|=N\ge2\), and \(U,V,W\) are affine maps with slopes \(1/4,1/6,1/9\), respectively, then
\[
|U(A)\cup V(A)\cup W(A)|\ge N+2.
\]

Suppose instead that the union \(B\) has at most \(N+1\) elements. Each image has \(N\) elements, and their diameters are different, so \(|B|\ne N\). Hence \(|B|=N+1\).

Write
\[
B=\{x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_N\},\qquad L=x_N-x_0.
\]
Each image omits exactly one element of \(B\). Omitting an interior element leaves diameter \(L\), while omitting an endpoint gives a smaller diameter. Since the three diameters are distinct, the largest image has diameter \(L\), and the other two images omit opposite endpoints. Their diameters are
\[
\frac23L,\qquad \frac49L.
\]

By reflecting \(B\) if necessary, suppose the image of diameter \(2L/3\) omits \(x_N\), and the image of diameter \(4L/9\) omits \(x_0\). Set
\[
d_i=x_i-x_{i-1}\quad(1\le i\le N).
\]
Then
\[
d_1=\frac59L,\qquad d_N=\frac13L.
\]
The two endpoint-deleted sets are affine images of the same set, with slope ratio \(2/3\). Consequently,
\[
d_{i+1}=\frac23d_i,
\]
giving
\[
\left(\frac23\right)^{N-1}=\frac{d_N}{d_1}=\frac35.
\]
This is impossible: clearing denominators would give
\[
5\cdot2^{N-1}=3^N.
\]
The claim follows.

In particular, whenever \(|A_n|\ge2\),
\[
|A_{n+1}|\ge |A_n|+2. \tag{1}
\]

### 2. Bound all nonzero choices of \((a,b,c)\)

Write the three inverse maps as
\[
F(x)=\frac14x+d_1,\qquad
G(x)=\frac16x+d_2,\qquad
H(x)=\frac19x+d_3.
\]
Thus \(A_1=\{d_1,d_2,d_3\}\).

#### Case 1: \(|A_1|=3\)

By (1),
\[
|A_{20}|\ge3+2(19)=41.
\]

#### Case 2: \(|A_1|=2\)

We show that \(|A_2|\ge5\).

Let the two maps sharing an intercept \(p\) have slopes \(u>v\), and let the remaining map have slope \(w\) and intercept \(q\ne p\). Put
\[
t=\frac{p}{q-p}.
\]
After dividing every element of \(A_2\) by \(q-p\), the six candidate values are
\[
(1+u)t,\quad (1+u)t+u,\quad
(1+v)t,\quad (1+v)t+v,\quad
(1+w)t+1,\quad (1+w)t+1+w.
\]
The two values within each displayed pair cannot coincide. Solving for collisions between different pairs gives the following possible values of \(t\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
(u,v,w)&\text{collision values of }t\\ \hline
(\frac14,\frac16,\frac19)&
0,-1,2,-3,\frac{36}{5},8,\frac{27}{5},\frac{31}{5},18,20,15,17\\[2pt]
(\frac14,\frac19,\frac16)&
0,-1,\frac45,-\frac95,12,14,9,11,-18,-21,-16,-19\\[2pt]
(\frac16,\frac19,\frac14)&
0,-1,2,-3,-12,-15,-10,-13,-\frac{36}{5},-9,-\frac{32}{5},-\frac{41}{5}
\end{array}
\]
Every entry in each row is distinct. Therefore, at any fixed \(t\), at most one pair of the six values coincides, so \(|A_2|\ge5\). Now (1) yields
\[
|A_{20}|\ge5+2(18)=41.
\]

#### Case 3: \(|A_1|=1\)

Here \(d_1=d_2=d_3=d\). If \(d=0\), all roots are \(0\), so \(R=1\).

If \(d\ne0\), the elements of \(A_3\) are
\[
d\bigl(1+s_i+s_is_j\bigr),
\qquad s_i,s_j\in\left\{\frac14,\frac16,\frac19\right\}.
\]
These nine values are distinct. Indeed, within each fixed \(s_i\), they are distinct, and the three groups are separated because
\[
\frac14\left(1+\frac19\right)>
\frac16\left(1+\frac14\right),
\qquad
\frac16\left(1+\frac19\right)>
\frac19\left(1+\frac14\right).
\]
Thus \(|A_3|=9\), and
\[
|A_{20}|\ge9+2(17)=43.
\]

We have proved that every value other than \(1\) is at least \(41\).

### 3. Attain the bound

Choose
\[
a=-3,\qquad b=-5,\qquad c=-8.
\]
Then all three original maps fix \(1\). A composition containing \(i\) copies of \(f\), \(j\) copies of \(g\), and \(k\) copies of \(h\), where \(i+j+k=20\), is
\[
x\longmapsto Mx+1-M,
\qquad M=4^i6^j9^k.
\]
Its root is \(1-1/M\). Moreover,
\[
M=2^{2i+j}3^{40-(2i+j)}.
\]
The integer \(2i+j\) takes every value from \(0\) through \(40\), giving exactly \(41\) distinct slopes and hence \(41\) distinct roots.

Since \(R=1\) is attained by \(a=b=c=0\), the second smallest possible value is
\[
\boxed{41}.
\]
